articles.title_orig: Owners of seized Russian oil tanker claim U.S. improperly sold ship for scrap metal
articles.title_zh: Owners of seized Russian oil tanker claim U.S. improperly sold ship for scrap metal
articles.content_orig:
U.S. authorities sold a seized Russian oil tanker to a maritime scrap dealer for well under market value in an “economically irrational” deal meant to thwart the owner’s bid to recover the vessel, the company lawyers said in court papers.
The Justice Department was ordered to respond to the allegations, made by the ship’s Russian owner, Burevestmarin LLC, by 9 a.m. Friday.
The tanker, Bella 1, was seized by the U.S. military in the North Atlantic in early January after a weekslong chase on the high seas. U.S. authorities said the ship, which they believed was carrying illegal Iranian oil, was caught fleeing an American blockade of Venezuela . Attorneys for Burevestmarin dispute the claim that the vessel was carrying Iranian oil.
The ship was sold to a scrap dealer for $9.1 million, the company’s lawyers said, well below the $21 million that the Bella 1 would fetch as scrap metal alone.
Even a proper scrap metal price tag would understate its worth, they added, because the ship has “substantially greater value” as “an operating commercial vessel.”
“As discussed and previously briefed, the Government posits a world in which it can — while withholding notice to known interested parties and while aware of challenges to the Court’s jurisdiction — engage in precisely this kind of economically irrational sale for its own convenience,”  the owner’s lawyers wrote.
They said the sale was conducted “behind closed doors” as part of the government’s “self-interested and unreasonable decisions.”
Representatives for the Justice Department and the scrap dealer named in court documents could not be immediately reached for comment Thursday.
Previously, DOJ attorneys have argued that seized ships put the government in a financial bind, so selling these vessels is necessary to avoid tens of millions of dollars in maintenance and repair costs.
DOJ attorney Rajbir Datta told the court in July that “the government has spent $60 million in maintaining this and doing all kinds of mechanical fixes to the asset itself.”
A root issue in the ongoing court battle is whether American authorities are right to argue that transporting Iranian oil benefits the sanctioned Islamic Revolutionary Guards Force.
That question is further complicated by the Trump administration permitting international sale of Iranian oil to help relieve domestic fuel prices.
Attorneys representing Bella 1’s owner are also fighting the Justice Department’s efforts to seize other ships that they own, citing what they believe is a legal double standard invoked by the government, court records show.
In the case of the vessel Galileo attorneys for the ship owner argued that “on March 20, 2026, the same day that the Government (under seal and ex parte) alleged that the Galileo was a source of influence over the IRGC and IRGC-QF, it expressly licensed the international sale of Iranian oil — an action that would be illegal under multiple statutes were the shipment of Iranian oil in itself necessarily the equivalent of providing a means of support to the IRGC or IRGC-QF or becoming the property of the IRGC or IRGC-QF.”
In the case of another vessel, Skipper, attorneys for Burevestmarin LLC said the Justice Department did not establish the correct venue and may have improperly seized that vessel. The Skipper was on the “high seas” thus meaning it was outside of the U.S. or a foreign country’s territorial waters.
Tom Winter is NBC’s National Law Enforcement and Intelligence Correspondent.

articles.title_orig: Chinese scientists chill atoms to record low on Tiangong space station
articles.title_zh: Chinese scientists chill atoms to record low on Tiangong space station
articles.content_orig:
Scientists brought thousands of rubidium atoms to less than 10 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero
That is about four times colder than the previous best, set in a German drop tower, and colder than anything reached by Nasa’s Cold Atom Lab on the International Space Station (ISS). The cloud held together for seven seconds, much longer than the two seconds achieved in the drop tower and about one second aboard the ISS.

articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
US first lady Melania Trump brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together at the White House on Thursday, calling on both sides to choose "humanity over war" ahead of talks next week in Abu Dhabi.
Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, attended the rare face-to-face gathering with Ukrainian officials. The event marked a six-day ceasefire that Melania Trump helped negotiate in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which expired on Sunday.
It came as the Trump administration is stepping up efforts to bring an end to Russia's war in Ukraine , which started when Russian troops invaded in early 2022. A trilateral meeting involving officials from the US, Ukraine, and Russia is set for November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.
"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady stated at the event. "We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people," she added.
Melania Trump said she was "involved in every stage of the planning" for the short-term ceasefire, which included reviewing aerial photos and evaluating road and hospital access.
President Trump, who did not attend, praised his wife’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire, remarking to reporters in October that "she does better than our professionals."
Dmitriev was expected to meet US officials while in Washington, according to two people familiar with his plans.
Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamia and human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets also attended the gathering. They encouraged the Slovenian-born Melania Trump to maintain her peace efforts.
Both delegations presented the first lady with gifts of appreciation.
Russia’s Dmitriev presented her with a drawing of pink hearts by an Oleshky girl, stating the child "chose to live with her family in Russia," alluding to the dispute over displaced Ukrainian children in Russia. "I love Melania," the artwork stated.
The Ukrainian delegation presented the first lady with a state honor "for your brave heart, for saving our people, and for returning back Ukrainian children."
She provided the visiting delegates with letters addressed to Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meeting was the first face-to-face contact between Russian and US officials following Tuesday's midterm elections, where Democrats won control of Congress from Republicans, dealing a blow to President Trump.
The incoming Democratic majority starting in January is expected to push for increased aid to Ukraine and scrutinize the Republican president's decisions to arrange a diesel deal with Russia and ease certain Moscow sanctions. Trump has heightened his criticism of Zelensky in recent weeks.
The Kremlin noted it hopes Trump will persist with his peace efforts despite the Republican Party’s loss.
It also stated preparations were under way for a summit between Putin, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China.
Dmitriev previously met Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, at the White House in 2025. Trump's predecessor, Joe Biden, did not invite Russian representatives to the White House.
Dmitriev has assisted in facilitating the release of American detainees in Russia, reuniting Ukrainian children with their families, and supporting the humanitarian effort in Oleshky.

articles.title_orig: FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Trump visits China
articles.title_zh: FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Trump visits China
articles.content_orig:
Iran celebrates its claimed role in ‘regime change’ amid pressure on Trump to ‘finish the job’ with attack
US midterms live – latest updates
I ran this week unveiled a huge billboard and banners over Enqelab Square in central Tehran. The billboard pledged in English: “We will kill Trump” – elevating the degree of personal animus with which Donald Trump is viewed in official Iranian circles.
The poster depicts the US president behind bars with his head bowed. And in a sense, given the US midterm election results on Tuesday, Iran has indeed killed Trump, or at least the second term of his presidency. Trump’s reverse is all the more piquant because it comes on the day Iran’s leadership celebrates the anniversary of the seizure of the US embassy in Tehran in 1979, an event that ensnared Jimmy Carter, and a reminder of how Iran has ruined the prospects of more than one US president.
Not surprisingly, the keenly followed election results have led to a good degree of triumphalism inside Iran .
Ehsan Movaheidian, an international relations scholar, claimed: “The Islamic Republic of Iran has succeeded in regime change in America. The same will soon happen in Europe as well. Bow down before the power of Iran.”
Meisam Zohurian, a conservative member of parliament, said: “The joy over the outcome of the US elections has nothing to do with the arrival of this party or the departure of that party. The issue is the aggressor was smeared in the dirt and Iran had an impact on the result.”
Ali Nikzad, the first deputy speaker of the parliament, said: “These electoral defeats are the aftershocks of Trump’s defeat by the Iranian people.”
Iran’s supreme leader said anyone expecting a shift in US policy was “seriously mistaken”, however. “Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Mojtaba Khamenei wrote.
Others predicted further electoral defeats for those they considered to be the warmongers in Europe, and the expulsion of US bases from the entire Middle East.
The resistance – or bloody-mindedness – shown by Iran for the past eight gruelling months did allow the strait of Hormuz to become an Iranian-controlled channel through which inflation and high diesel prices were transmitted to the US system. Even Trump himself on Wednesday accepted, and lamented, that the American people had decided the “short-term” pain of inflation was not a price worth paying to prevent Iran becoming a nuclear power.
But the big question now is whether either side will regard these seismic results as a moment to review their diplomatic strategy. Iran’s chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, was quick to call on Trump to accept the wisdom of the American people. On social media he urged Trump to bow to the verdict of America: “Whether driven by conscience or the cost of living, America said no to war and we endorse this message.”
Ghalibaf added: “If the US government betrays the public will in order to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our ‘no’ comes with a nightmare.”
Yet Iran will also be asked to reflect on the wisdom of war by the Gulf monarchies, and possibly by Russia and China – the latter a country that finally seems to be stirring itself to find a solution to the blockade in the strait of Hormuz which is preventing badly needed Middle East oil exports from reaching its industries.
China tends to knock only on doors it knows are going to open, so it is probably testing the feasibility of a deal in which Iran “downblends” – or dilutes – its stockpile of highly enriched uranium inside Iran under international supervision. A Chinese special envoy is travelling to Oman, Iran and Saudi Arabia almost immediately.
These countries, some sympathetic to Iran’s predicament, can point out that if Tehran ever thought in the run-up to the elections Trump would capitulate and turn his carrier fleet around, it was mistaken. Some Iranian diplomats had indeed hoped that the prospect of defeat in the midterms, and pressure from within the Republican party, would have led Trump to make concessions to Tehran.
after newsletter promotion
In fact, both sides and the chief mediator, Qatar, clearly did try to use polling day as a lever, but in the end neither retreated. Trump, for once, was true to his word and refused to allow the darkening opinion polls to reduce his determination to keep Iran in his vice. Confined to a holding bay of “neither war nor peace”, Trump’s priority was to keep the oil price as low as possible by repeatedly suggesting a settlement might be imminent.
For the next two months before the new Congress convenes in January – so reducing his budgetary options – Trump has greater latitude, and little accountability. The damage to the Republican party has been done and cannot be undone.
Unsurprisingly the Trump influencers who advocated for the war in the first place are piling on pressure to strike again quickly. Laura Loomer wrote on X: “Time for President Trump to deal with Iran once and for all. Just do it, Nothing to lose now. Finish the job.”
But the credibility of Loomer and her like has been severely damaged: in February, she advised Trump that regime change in Iran – “a little excursion” – could be as easy as knocking over the Maduro regime in Venezuela. Similarly, Benjamin Netanyahu is now touting intelligence showing that Iran is preparing to use chemical weapons. The ease with which the Israeli prime minister conjures up intelligence to justify another assault on Iran may by now have struck the White House.
Hillary Clinton, Trump’s old sparring partner, is one who thinks Trump will probably launch the long-delayed attack. She said: “I think he will feel trapped. He will feel angry and resentful and he will react aggressively.”
Having come so far, and paid so high a political price, Trump may in the next two months try to secure a legacy by finishing the job – however he defines that. He is convinced, as he told Fox News this week, that “Iran has very few missiles and drones left, and even less capacity to build any more”. He crowed: “We are dealing with total strength. We can end it any time.”
Unfortunately, such blithe optimism has been heard before.

articles.title_orig: New wave of bomb hoaxes hits at least 27 passenger flights across Europe
articles.title_zh: New wave of bomb hoaxes hits at least 27 passenger flights across Europe
articles.content_orig:
Planes forced into emergency landings or diversions two days after hoax alerts affected air travel
Europe live – latest updates
Hoax bomb threats have caused at least 25 flights across Europe to be disrupted, with some forced to make emergency landings, as questions mount over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.
The series of warnings on Thursday affected flights between Italy, Ireland, the UK, Spain, Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Finland, Austria, Denmark, Belgium, Portugal, France, Greece, Serbia and Czechia.
The threats affected flights by Ryanair, Aer Lingus, Wizz Air, Finnair, easyJet, Aegean Airlines, Iberia, Sky Express, Air Serbia and LOT Polish Airlines. All landed safely. Searches of the planes found nothing suspicious.
In the UK, Heathrow, London’s principal airport, and Birmingham airport received threats overnight, but it was determined that they were hoaxes with the help of specialist investigators from the Metropolitan police’s aviation police command.
The day of hoaxes followed similar threats on Tuesday, when seven planes across Europe were searched or diverted after malicious alerts. On Monday a flight from the UK to Bulgaria was diverted after a threat that was apparently without substance. In total at least 33 flights have been affected this week.
Investigators said on Thursday there remained no evidence that the hoaxes were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, although inquiries across Europe into the incidents continue.
The global airlines body Iata condemned the disruption and urged authorities to identify the origin of the threats. “Safety is the number one priority for the industry and we take all threats seriously,” said Nick Careen, Iata’s senior vice-president for operations, safety and security, in a statement.
The EU transport commissioner, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, said it was too early to know if the incidents were linked but that any threats against civilians were unacceptable.
Bomb threats emailed to airports in Rome and Sofia were signed “fighters of the Male State”, according to sources at Aeroporti di Roma, which manages the city’s two airports, and a text seen by Agence France-Presse.
Male State is a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016 by Vladislav Pozdnyakov. On his Telegram channel Pozdnyakov, a prominent supporter of the war in Ukraine, did not comment on or claim responsibility for the bomb threats.
The emails reportedly read: “We, the fighters of the Male State, will make history with our actions today. Your feminist regime will remember this for ever. The explosion will occur in 60 minutes. Today, your skies will turn red.”
A Cork airport spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the airport had received an anonymous threat by phone on Thursday morning, causing a flight to be delayed. It was understood to be a Ryanair flight from London Stansted.
A separate Ryanair flight from Pescara in Italy to Brussels-Charleroi was inspected after the word “bomb” was discovered scrawled on the walls of its onboard toilet.
The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny fraction of the 27,400 flights scheduled in Europe on Thursday, according to the European air traffic control agency, Eurocontrol .
The pilot of an Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome that diverted to Évreux was being questioned by French authorities for initially refusing to land at a military base, according to French media reports.
The disruption followed cyber-attacks this week against supermarket refrigeration systems .
A Kremlin spokesperson said on Thursday it was “absurd” to blame Vladimir Putin’s administration for the fridge hacks. “We have ​such baseless accusations against our country, implicating it in everything,” Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
In Rome, Guido Crosetto, the Italian defence minister, said: “It seems to me that every day now, from refrigerators to blood supplies in France, to these fake alarms, there’s someone who has an interest in stoking tensions.”
Asked if he knew who was behind the hoaxes, he said: “It’s called ‘under-threshold warfare’ because it’s below the attribution threshold. It’s done that way on purpose, so no one can pin the blame.”
Many of the affected flights were operated by low-cost carriers but there was little discernible pattern surrounding the incidents.
Aviation experts say fake threats occur daily but that such a number of credible threats, even if malicious hoaxes, appears to point to coordinated action.
Capt Martin Drake, a former airline pilot and technical adviser to the British Airline Pilots’ Association union, said airlines had security teams who assessed each threat on a traffic-light scale: green to keep going or red to be grounded, with an amber option only for flights yet to take off, allowing tighter checks and searches of the plane before clearing it to fly.
“If you want to deliberately disrupt a flight, then you need to do so once it’s airborne,” said Drake. Pilots have a QRH – a quick response handbook – whose instructions will probably include to descend quickly as well as divert to the nearest airport on receipt of a red alert.
At cruising altitude, “aircraft pressurisation would do a lot of the work of any improvised explosive device”.
While getting a large explosive onboard should be ruled out by multiple layers of security and screening, the effects of any detonation would be multiplied for planes at typical cruising altitude of 35,000ft.
Diversions are expensive as well as highly disruptive, but airlines have little choice in the face of any remotely credible threat.
The ready availability of airline operations information on the internet means that any hoaxer now has a level of detail about the schedules, the type of plane and its technical specifications that would have eluded all but insiders decades ago.
Rhys Jones, an analyst at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation intelligence firm, said the confidence of airlines in European airport security should not mean any change to normal protocols after the hoaxes, but “one of the natural responses will be to see double-downed security, media coverage and public concern about travelling”.
He said the threats seemed linked but “a reasonably chaotic campaign with no particular region targeted”, and while they could weaken future security responses through the normalisation of threats, simply creating disruption could be regarded as a success by those carrying out the hoaxes.
Additional reporting by Dan Sabbagh in London, Pjotr Sauer in Amsterdam and Angela Giuffrida in Rome

articles.title_orig: Paraguayan president impeached minutes after resigning following bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguayan president impeached minutes after resigning following bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank, which Paraguay's central bank seized amid a solvency crisis, in Asunción, Paraguay, Wednesday. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguay's lower house voted unanimously Thursday to impeach President Santiago Peña just minutes after he announced his resignation, as the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings, sent protesters surging into the streets and turned his own party against him.
The 78-0 vote marked a stunning repudiation of Peña by lawmakers from his long-ruling Colorado Party, who joined the opposition in backing his impeachment after three days of demonstrations rocked the capital, Asunción. The vote sends the charges to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is required to convict the president and formally remove him from office.
The impeachment came as thousands protested for a third day, as they attempt to recoup lost savings, wages and pensions from Ueno Bank, a major digital lender.
Peña, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
Paraguay President Santiago Peña speaks to the media at United Nations headquarters, Sept. 19, 2023. Ted Shaffrey/AP hide caption
The president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.
"I also want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The extraordinary turn of events set the stage for a transfer of power later Thursday. Congress was expected to formally accept Peña's resignation at 5 p.m., clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in as president an hour later. Alliana would serve out Peña's term through August 2028, with lawmakers expected to choose a new vice president.
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.
Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno's holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left.
Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña's request.
Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.
Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank's parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.
"We want your head, Peña!" they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña's impeachment, called him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.
Many demonstrators saw Ueno's collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.
"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said protester Belarmino Balbuena.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.

articles.content_orig:
President Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.
The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
The documents show the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."
"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.
"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."
"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal."
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis took credit for disrupting travel using a drone at King Fahd International Airport on Thursday.
"We targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam using a drone and our operation caused a disruption of air navigation at the airport," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.
The city of Dammam, which is located in the oil-rich eastern part of Saudi Arabia, and King Fahd airport have been regular targets for Houthi attacks. Multiple drones have disrupted traffic at the airport this week, according to past announcements.
Two people were killed in a Houthi strike on King Fahd airport on Oct. 22.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its associated strike group will make a port call in Singapore Friday and will not reach the Middle East for at least another two weeks, a U.S. official told CBS News on Thursday.
There are already two carrier strike groups in the region and, which officials say is sufficient firepower to execute any commands issued by President Trump.
Mr. Trump has not signaled yet, in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, whether he intends to order major new strikes on Iran — an option he kept on the table with repeated statements ahead of Tuesday's voting.
The initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit Thursday.
The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, considered the international standard, rose 2.2% to $96.70, recovering a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before.
Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, met Thursday in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin to deliver a message from Iran's supreme leader, according to the Iranian government.
They met amid uncertainty over President Trump's next move on Iran in the wake of U.S. midterm election results that represented a major rebuke of his policies, including, he has admitted, the decision to launch the war with Iran alongside Israel more than eight months ago.
Mr. Trump said repeatedly ahead of the Tuesday vote that he had yet to make a decision on whether to order major new attacks on Iran or to agree a deal to end the war, which Tehran has so far refused to do until the U.S. accepts its core demands to end its naval blockade, ensure a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, and ease sanctions.
During the Rezaei-Putin meeting in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned Russian citizens against all travel to Iran.
"Given the continued risk of a new escalation around Iran, our recommendations to Russian citizens remain unchanged," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters in Moscow. "We recommend temporarily refraining from traveling to that country until the situation is resolved. We also ask our compatriots already in Iran to exercise vigilance and avoid crowds, public events, and areas near military and government facilities."
She said the guidance was "based on the official information disseminated by Tehran," without providing any further detail.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry renewed the regime's rejection on Thursday of longtime and widely held beliefs that Tehran materially supports the Houthi rebels fighting the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen's decade-long civil war. The conflict intensified a couple months ago and quickly became the most active and deadly front in the intertwined conflicts in the Middle East.
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the latest accusation of Iranian support for the Houthis, made Monday by European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, "baseless," and said Iran "strongly denied claims that Iranian military experts were present in Yemen."
The U.S. government, along with many other Western nations and the NATO alliance , have demanded for years that Iran stop supporting the Houthis. The support, according to these nations, includes financial backing, weapons and other equipment, and direct coordination and training.
In July, not long before the Yemen war escalated and the Houthis started launching attacks on Saudi airports in response, the Reuters news agency reported that Iran  had flown commanders from its powerful, heavily sanctioned Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, along with equipment related to missiles and drones, to Yemen bolster the Houthis' ability to threaten global energy supplies in the Red Sea.
Since then, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabian airports have killed at least 20 people.
In her remarks Monday, the EU's Kallas said "all Houthi military action must end immediately. We call on all actors, including Iran to cease all military support to the Houthis, in violation of several United Nations Security Council resolutions."
Iran has always denied supporting the Houthis.
Oman's government said Thursday that, in a phone call between the Omani and Iranian foreign ministers, both men "stressed the importance of moving from the stage of de-escalating tensions to one of establishing sustainable understandings based on practical arrangements to ensure the safety of maritime routes and joint technical mechanisms to secure the smooth flow of international trade and energy, in a manner that would end the state of war and prevent renewed confrontations in the region."
Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamoud Al Busaidi and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi "reviewed the latest developments in communications and discussions aimed at reaching practical, political, and technical understandings that would enable the resumption of unimpeded maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," the Omani Foreign Ministry said in a statement .
Iran and Oman have discussed for months implementing a joint mechanism to control commercial traffic through the strait, over which both Iran and the U.S. insist they currently have dominion. Iran started threatening and attacking ships in the region in response to the U.S. and Israel jointly launching the ongoing war against the Islamic Republic at the end of February, and those attacks continue despite U.S. assertions that the strait is now open safe to use.

articles.title_orig: Iran is Reviewing ‘Concrete Proposals’ on Nuclear Program, Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Iran is Reviewing ‘Concrete Proposals’ on Nuclear Program, Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process “.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack .
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.title_orig: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.title_zh: Bomb threats hit multiple flights in Europe for a second time in a week
articles.content_orig:

Bomb threats across Europe have grounded flights across several countries and caused travel disruptions on Thursday.
It marks the second time this week that such widespread threats have been reported prompting fear and concern against the backdrop of a series of cyber-attacks affecting supermarket fridges and blood banks across the continent.
Flights flying to and from the UK , Belgium , Ireland, Italy , Finland , Bulgaria , Spain and Denmark were impacted and were largely resolved by the end of the day.
More than a dozen flights were targeted, included those from Copenhagen , Dublin , Helsinki , Madrid, Milan and Warsaw.
A Finnair plane from Helsinki was safely escorted to its scheduled landing in Rome by Italian Air Force jets. A Ryanair aircraft landed at Sofia airport after planes flying from Copenhagen and Madrid landed in the Bulgarian capital, according to the country’s interior minister.
Inspections of three Ryanair aircraft that received bomb threats and landed at the Bulgarian airports did not identify any issues, the country’s transport ministry said.
“Upon landing, the necessary inspections were carried out in accordance with the applicable procedures and no issues were identified,” the country’s transport ministry told Reuters. Airport operations at both Sofia and Plovdiv airports have returned to normal, it said.
Airports in the UK were also impacted amid threats reported at Heathrow and Birmingham airports.
“Threats reported at Heathrow and Birmingham in the early hours of this morning have been resolved,” a government spokesperson said in a statement issued on Thursday.
“It’s right that authorities treat any potential threats seriously — the UK has one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any threats, as well as malicious hoaxes, like those we’ve seen this week.”
The Times reported that the Metropolitan Police are continuing to monitor the situation.
Finnair also said that its two affected flights had landed safely after being affected by bomb threats.
Flights AY1761 from Helsinki to Rome and AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, faced unfounded or hoax bomb threats, the company said.
“Both flights landed safely at their destinations, and customers have disembarked the aircraft,” it said and added that nothing suspicious was found on the planes.
The plane to Rome was inspected and will depart back to Helsinki, while the flight to Vienna will “return to traffic normally after inspection.”
The incidents followed hoax bomb threats earlier this week that prompted searches, diversions and, in one case, a military escort across at least seven flights in Europe. An airport in Poland was forced to close in a day of chaos on Tuesday.
“Malicious” bomb scares on two flights from London , and others from Manchester, Copenhagen, Israel , Dublin, Bergamo and Lisbon threw airports into disarray, with authorities searching planes after some of the flights were forced to undergo emergency landings.
Hundreds of passengers on board were affected as well as others who had been affected by the temporary closures of airports.
On Wednesday, the French health ministry said that blood banks in France had been hit by a cyberattack amid a series of online hoaxes and cyberattacks.
“Several regional facilities of the French Blood Establishment (EFS) were affected by a cybersecurity incident that impacted certain cold storage room monitoring and control systems,” the ministry said.
Meanwhile, stores in eight European countries were forced to throw away vast quantities of food after hackers tampered with their fridges on Monday, mirroring hacks that swept dozens of supermarkets in France three weeks ago.

articles.title_orig: Gamers go to ridiculous lengths to “improve” GTA VI with Nvidia’s DLSS 5
articles.title_zh: Gamers go to ridiculous lengths to “improve” GTA VI with Nvidia’s DLSS 5
articles.content_orig:
While the upcoming Grand Theft Auto VI won’t be available on PC this month, some gamers are making ridiculous preparations to use their PC graphics cards to apply Nvidia’s DLSS 5 technology to the console exclusive.
On an explicitly unmoderated GTAVI subreddit, user RevolutionaryBus8208 lays out a proposed setup, which runs a PlayStation 5 through a 4K capture card to a PC. From there, the video signal is run through Veyra , an open source tool that can apply DLSS 5’s AI-powered “neural rendering” to video content. The result—which also uses DLSS frame generation to increase the 30 fps source to a 90 fps output—is then piped back to a 4K TV, theoretically adding some of the benefits of a beefy PC graphics card to a console-exclusive game.
To demonstrate the potential of this setup, RevolutionaryBus8208 used Veyra to upscale the Grand Theft Auto VI Extended Look trailer posted in August. The resulting DLSS-ified version looks a bit better in places, with sharper background elements, subtler shadows, and more believable light scattering on some surfaces. But it also seems a bit washed out compared to the original video’s deeper blacks and arguably suffers from an unnaturally smooth “soap opera effect” in some scenes.
While the upscaled version causes some occasional graphical artifacts and glitches from the frame generation process, it’s still an interesting proof of concept that shows just how far DLSS 5 has come from some of the early horror-show memes that circulated on the Internet earlier this year.
Of course, running this kind of remote frame generation on a linear video is very different from applying it to a real-time interactive game. While a pure “passthrough” capture card wouldn’t necessarily add any latency itself, any software processing done to get the video feed ready for upscaling—and to do the upscaling itself—could add significant delays between player inputs and on-screen results.
RevolutionaryBus8208 claims that Veyra itself adds a relatively small 11 ms of additional latency to the video source but admits he doesn’t have a capture card to test it with a signal coming from an actual PS5. Other commenters who have tried similar setups with other PS5 games said the input lag was “noticeable but tolerable” or claimed an impossible-to-believe latency addition of “around 1-2 milliseconds.”
For players who can already use Sony’s “PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution” on a PS5 Pro, going through this convoluted process might cause a “hat on a hat” effect. But for stock PS5 owners who happen to have a beefy PC GPU, the hassles and trade-offs might be worth it to get some additional horsepower on console exclusives like GTA VI .
Or, you know, you could just wait for the game’s actual PC release, which is reportedly slated for early 2027 . Or for the likely AI-assisted unofficial decompilation port that should be along any day now.

articles.title_orig: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: How Melania Trump Became a Dark Horse Diplomat on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump .
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war . It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.
Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
Aidan  Stretch contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Communist Party of Vietnam delegation pays working visit to China
articles.title_zh: Communist Party of Vietnam delegation pays working visit to China
articles.content_orig:
A delegation of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) led by Nguyen Thanh Nghi, member of the Political Bureau, Secretary of the CPV Central Committee, and head of the committee’s Commission for Policy and Strategy, paid a working visit to China from November 1 to 5. The visit followed the fifth plenary session of the 20th central committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC).
Nghi met with Wang Huning, member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC); held talks with He Lifeng, member of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, Vice Premier, and Director of the Office of the Central Commission for Financial and Economic Affairs; and had a working session with Lu Hao, member of the CPC Central Committee and Director of the Development Research Centre of the State Council of China.
He congratulated China on its tremendous and comprehensive development achievements and the success of the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, held from October 26–29, describing it as an important theoretical preparation for the CPC’s 21st National Congress. He further expressed confidence that China would successfully implement the Resolution of the 20th National Congress of the CPC, successfully convene the 21st National Congress, and achieve its goal of building China into a modern socialist country that is prosperous, strong, democratic, culturally advanced, harmonious and beautiful.
Nghi also briefed the Chinese side on the implementation of the resolution of Vietnam’s 14th National Party Congress and the country’s socio-economic development, as well as several key policies and orientations adopted at the fourth plenum of the Party Central Committee.
Highlighting the long-standing friendship between Vietnam and China and Vietnam’s policy of giving top priority to developing ties with China, he affirmed that the Vietnamese Party and State stand ready to work with their Chinese counterparts to further strengthen political trust, enhance strategic connectivity, elevate substantive cooperation and support each other in their respective development processes.
Appreciating the significance of the visit, which followed a series of exchanges and meetings between the two countries’ high-ranking leaders, the Chinese leaders affirmed that China always regards relations with Vietnam as a priority in its neighbourhood diplomacy and supports Vietnam in playing a greater international role.
The two sides spoke highly of the positive and comprehensive progress in Vietnam-China relations and agreed to strengthen the leadership and guidance of the two Parties over ministries, sectors, agencies and localities in both countries.
China welcomed Vietnam’s participation in its ‘Big Market for All: Export to China’ initiative. It also expressed readiness to further increase imports of Vietnamese agricultural products and support capable Chinese enterprises in expanding investment in Vietnam.
Following the talks in Beijing the delegation visited Hangzhou, the capital of Zhejiang province.

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid from activist investor and adopts 'poison pill' plan - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low, and it adopted a “poison pill” plan that would make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May from Potbelly, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose more than 2% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance during the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.
Wendy's also announced that it has adopted a shareholders' rights plan, a so-called “poison pill,” intended to avert a hostile takeover of the company. The plan, which grants all shareholders except the hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares, automatically triggers if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said. Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Wendy’s, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy's is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.

articles.title_orig: Oman Sultan, Iran and Saudi envoys visit China
articles.title_zh: Oman Sultan, Iran and Saudi envoys visit China
articles.content_orig:
At the invitation of President Xi Jinping, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said of Oman paid a state visit to China from November 1 to 2. This was the first China visit by an Omani head of state since diplomatic ties were established 48 years ago in 1978.
Ding Long, a professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University, told Global Times that with tensions mounting in the Strait of Hormuz, and Oman, which has been a long-standing active mediator in regional disputes, coming under pressure as well, the visit reflects the country’s efforts to strengthen strategic support and enhance diplomatic autonomy.
Oman is the only member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) to consistently maintain positive relations with Iran, and it has played a pivotal role in regional diplomacy, including hosting rounds of talks between Iran and the United States. Its peaceful policy has earned at least one threat from US President Donald Trump to bomb the country.
Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks with Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik Al Said on November 2. He said that China stands ready to work with Oman to steer their strategic partnership to a higher level, and to help restore peace and realise lasting stability in the Middle East at an early date. China and Oman, he added, should enhance political mutual trust and strengthen exchanges of experience in national governance, while expressing China’s support for Oman in safeguarding national independence, sovereignty, security and stability, and in independently exploring a development path suited to its national conditions. And China, he said, is ready to deepen the synergy of development strategies with Oman and to be a stable and reliable partner in the energy sector, a partner with promising potential in investment, and a partner in fostering innovation in advanced technologies.
“China has been actively committed to ending hostilities and promoting peace, aiming to contribute its wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security predicament,” Xi said, adding that China will continue to advocate resolving disputes through political and diplomatic means, and support regional countries in building a common home of good-neighbourliness, development, security and cooperation.
Stressing that China has been Oman’s largest trading partner for many years and Chinese enterprises’ investment in Oman has kept growing, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik said his country is ready to synergise development strategies with China and strengthen cooperation in trade, investment, industry, infrastructure, AI, science and technology, and other fields. He said Oman highly appreciates China’s just position on the Middle East issue and stands ready to maintain close coordination with China to uphold international law, advocate for the peaceful resolution of disputes, and jointly promote security and stability in the region and beyond.
Later that day, Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik met with Chinese Premier Li Qiang. Li said the talks between the two heads of state earlier that morning mapped out a new blueprint for further deepening the China-Oman strategic partnership. He expressed China’s willingness to strengthen the alignment of development strategies with Oman, deepen cooperation across the entire oil and gas industry chain, and carry out more high-quality clean energy projects and called on both sides to expand cooperation in areas such as agriculture and fisheries, aerospace satellites, information and communication, and artificial intelligence, and promote the early conclusion of the free trade agreement negotiations between China and the GCC. He stressed that China and Oman, both Global South countries, should maintain close communication and coordination in multilateral affairs to jointly safeguard world peace and stability.
Sultan Haitham Bin Tarik said Oman deeply admires China’s development achievements, which have attracted attention worldwide. Oman looks forward to learning from China’s development experience and deepening mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries. Oman is willing to enhance communication and coordination with China in international and regional affairs and to contribute to resolving conflicts and maintaining peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region.
In a potentially significant but under-reported related development, also on November 2, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met separately with the Deputy Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and the National Security Advisor of Saudi Arabia.
Meeting with Deputy Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Ali Bagheri Kani, Wang Yi stated that China-Iran relations have maintained steady development despite a volatile international landscape. This serves the fundamental interests of both peoples and reflects the aspirations of Global South countries for solidarity and cooperation. China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security and is willing to work with Iran to further advance bilateral relations.
Ali Bagheri Kani briefed Wang Yi on Iran’s views concerning the regional situation, stating that Iran would firmly safeguard its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, and resist power politics and threats. Iran is also willing to engage in talks and negotiations with all parties and work actively for regional peace and stability. The Iranian side appreciates the initiatives and proposals put forward by President Xi Jinping and China’s consistent commitment to multilateralism. Iran looks forward to China playing a greater role in international and regional peace. Iran stands ready to promote the steady development of bilateral ties and to strengthen cooperation with China in international and multilateral frameworks.
In his meeting with Wang Yi, Saudi Arabia’s Minister of State, Member of the Council of Ministers, and National Security Advisor Musaad bin Mohammed Al-Aiban handed over a letter from Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman to President Xi Jinping regarding the development of China-Saudi bilateral relations and issues of mutual concern.
Wang Yi said that the current regional situation has once again reached a critical crossroads between war and peace. Although the road to peace is not smooth, it is necessary to keep moving forward. He hoped that all parties would resolve disputes and end the conflict through dialogue and negotiation, safeguarding regional energy and shipping security. China believes that countries in the region should enhance understanding, rebuild mutual trust, improve relations, and live harmoniously, promoting the construction of a new regional security framework that serves the long-term interests of their peoples through consultation.

articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The selloff came a day after the Dow soared more than 1,500 points.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged about 1,200 points on Thursday, eroding most of the rally from a day earlier when midterm election results propelled the index to its best trading session in more than a year.
The S & P 500 dropped 3.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 4.8%, putting the index into correction territory, meaning it has fallen more than 10% from a previous peak last month.
The Dow declined 1,220 points, or 2.2%.
The selloff hammered many artificial intelligence firms as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.
Nvidia, the chipmaking giant behind many of the semiconductors used in AI products, dropped 7% on Thursday. Rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices saw shares fall 12%. SanDisk, another AI hardware firm, plummeted more than 15% in value.
The slide also hit some other major tech firms behind AI development.
Microsoft, which holds a large stake in OpenAI, saw its stock price fall more than 2%. Amazon, which has spent hundreds of billions on its build-out of AI infrastructure, also dropped more than 2%.
The downturn in markets largely reversed blockbuster gains from the previous session.
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 1,570 points, or 3%, recording its best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, when President Donald Trump announced the suspension of a far-reaching set of reciprocal tariffs.
Even as stocks climbed on Wednesday, Yorkville analyst Dan Ives warned ABC News of potential midterm fallout for the tech sector.
"The Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years," Ives told ABC News in a statement.
Tuesday's midterm elections catapulted Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers.
A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber.
OpenAI unveiled a new set of data center policies Thursday for that it called "responsible AI infrastructure" in the aftermath of the election.
The ChatGPT maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It also will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," and will "create opportunities for local workers and businesses" for employment, the AI company said in a blog post .

articles.title_orig: So, about that Anthropic IPO . . .
articles.title_zh: So, about that Anthropic IPO . . .
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX’s SPCX recent IPO may have raised some investors’ hopes of using mutual and exchange-traded funds to capture any pop in Anthropic’s pending offering, but they’re unlikely to reap life-changing riches that way.
First, most funds already mark their positions near the expected IPO value, limiting upside potential. Second, most funds’ stakes in the Claude chatbot creator are very small, meaning the portfolios’ other, larger holdings will water down any gains. Finally, as SpaceX showed, early IPO pops can deflate quickly, and timing postoffering sales is not easy.
Funds’ per-share, split-adjusted Anthropic values ranged from Franklin Templeton’s $58.90, as of its Sept. 30, 2026, portfolios, to T. Rowe Price’s $91.65, as of Oct. 30—a massive 55% difference. Timing could explain some of the gap; Franklin’s calculation appears to reflect Anthropic’s last May 2026 financing round price, without subsequent adjustments. It’s possible the firm has revised its numbers since the frontier artificial intelligence lab filed its S-1 IPO prospectus in October.
Still, timing does not account for all differences. Looking only at Sept. 30 portfolios, per-share values ranged from ClearBridge Select Fund’s LBFIX $58.90 (ClearBridge is a subsidiary of Franklin Templeton), seemingly reflecting Anthropic’s last financing round, to Tema Electrification ETF’s VOLT $85.10—a still-massive 44% difference. Given that Anthropic’s last financing round in May 2026 valued the company at $965 billion, that implies a $400 billion to $500 billion gap between ClearBridge’s estimated Anthropic value versus Tema’s and T. Rowe’s marks, a gap roughly equivalent to the size of the 20th largest company in the S&P 500.
Assuming those values have not converged, ClearBridge’s discounted Anthropic valuation relative to Tema or T. Rowe seems to offer an opportunity to realize more appreciation if the AI company’s shares jump after its IPO. Given recent reporting that Anthropic is targeting a $1.5 trillion valuation, outside of the ClearBridge fund, much of the upside is already baked into mutual funds and ETFs’ net asset values, so there are no massive gains to be had for investors based purely on the expected IPO price.
Why do these valuations vary so much? Mutual funds and ETFs have significant leeway in valuing private companies, since such holdings rarely have observable trading prices. In practice, many asset managers anchor to the most recent financing round (Anthropic last raised money in May at a $965 billion valuation, or about $589 per share) and adjust based on market conditions or big secondary market trades. That still leaves a lot of room for disagreement among fund firms, especially when AI-related stocks post wide daily swings, as they have recently. As a result, valuation is often in the eye of the beholder.
Reported valuations can be stale, too. Mutual funds often disclose their portfolios 30 days after month- or quarter-end, so the Anthropic valuations we see could be different from what funds think it is worth in real time. Anthropic also disclosed in its S-1 that it did a 10-for-1 share split in September, so reported per-share valuations can also look 10 times higher than they truly are.
In addition to the potential return difference that different valuations can cause, investors seeking pre-IPO exposure to Anthropic should note most funds and ETFs do not have large Anthropic positions. Only one has more than 5% of its portfolio in the company, and even at that level, the AI lab could double its value and the fund would see just a 5% gain, before factoring in how the other 95% of the portfolio performs.
Of course, there is also no guarantee that Anthropic’s stock will rise post-IPO, and potential share price volatility can make timing an exit even harder, as SpaceX has shown. Despite SpaceX’s massive rally in its first few days of trading (it nearly doubled by its third day of trading), it now trades near its IPO offer price.
Thus, given funds’ and ETFs’ small helpings of Anthropic, the baked-in valuations, and the uncertainty over the direction, magnitude, and duration of its shares’ post-IPO performance, it’s not worth it for most investors to buy a mutual fund or ETF simply to get short-term exposure to Anthropic’s historic IPO.

articles.title_orig: Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design
articles.title_zh: Xbox overhauls its PC, web, and cloud apps with a faster design
articles.content_orig:
Xbox Insiders can start testing the new PC app today.
Xbox Insiders can start testing the new PC app today.
Microsoft is unveiling a new Xbox PC app that launches “up to 60 percent faster” than before, with an overhauled design to match new updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and smart TVs. Xbox Insiders will be able to start testing the updated Xbox PC app today, and the updated Xbox Cloud Gaming interface will start rolling out over the next few weeks.
Ever since Microsoft launched its Xbox Ally handheld devices last year, it was clear the Xbox PC app still needed a lot of work to feel more like an Xbox console experience on Windows. Microsoft has greatly simplified the app now, with a design that no longer feels like you’re clicking a mouse when you’re using a controller.
“The app now launches up to 60 percent faster,” says Jason Beaumont , VP of Xbox experiences. “Pages like Home, Store, and Game Pass load up to 50 percent faster, and in-app windows open up to 65 percent faster.” The Xbox PC app also has simplified navigation that should make it easier to use on a controller, and the library section now has updated filters and better ways to organize your installed games.
Microsoft has improved the social parts of the Xbox PC app, too, with friends now listed in the main page and quick buttons to start a chat or join a party. The app overall feels less like a web one now, with what appears to be a mix of native and web elements. Microsoft has also refreshed the game card UI, as well as the home and settings sections. Even the animations have been updated to make this feel more like an Xbox dashboard experience.
I’ve been using this new Xbox PC app for the past few weeks, and it’s noticeably faster on a variety of devices I own. I’ve found it’s much easier to navigate around with a controller, and the search interface no longer tries to pop up when you’re moving between sections.
This redesign does make the Game Bar interface on handhelds feel a little out of place now, though. I understand Microsoft is looking to improve that in the coming months, and there should be design updates to make it match more closely to this updated Xbox PC app.
This new UI is also coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming. “We’re also bringing the refreshed Xbox web experience to more players and rolling out updates to Xbox Cloud Gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets,” says Beaumont. “These changes are part of our work to make Xbox faster, simpler, and more familiar wherever you play.”
The refreshed web version of Xbox Cloud Gaming has a similar look and feel to the Xbox PC app. A new library tab highlights cloud games across your own library and Xbox Game Pass. A desktop mode makes better use of larger displays, and you can choose between dark and light modes, as well as five new high-contrast options designed to improve accessibility support.
A similar design will also be available on smart TVs and VR headsets soon, but these designs aren’t exactly the same across PC, web, and smart TVs as Microsoft has customized them. “Playing on a PC, TV, or VR headset is different, and each experience needs to work well for the screen you’re using,” says Beaumont. “Wherever you play, the basics should feel familiar: finding your games, knowing what you can play, and getting into a game quickly.”
