articles.title_orig: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.title_zh: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.content_orig:
BREAKING: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman unseats Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, another win for the left in a major city
Shares in technology companies dropped sharply Thursday, compounding recent declines and sparking concerns about the durability of an artificial intelligence boom that has driven much of recent U.S. economic growth.
The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped as much as 6.2%, before rebounding to trade lower by about 4.5% throughout the late morning.
The S&P 500 also rebounded from earlier losses, but was still down 3.1%, putting it on track for its worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, also entered “correction” territory on Thursday, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%.
Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for AI’s development and operation.
Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq has surged almost 40%.
But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months.
“I don’t think this is an AI bubble bursting,” said Ed Yardeni, longtime market watcher and president of Yardeni Research. “I think it’s an AI bubble losing some air very, very rapidly, and I think that reduces the likelihood that we’ll get a bursting  bubble that has adverse consequences for the economy and broader financial system.”
Also contributing to losses were the commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers.
Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets.
“Today is the cold shower that I anticipated might occur after a blue-wave situation,” Yardeni said.
Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid nearly 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. But the two companies are also engaged in developing AI, and SpaceX has recently emerged as a data center developer.
Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories.
Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels.
The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed.
The two companies were among the worst performers on the Nasdaq indexes, sliding 12%.
Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector.
Memory and chip firms SanDisk, Western Digital, AMD, Seagate and Micron were among the S&P 500’s biggest losers, all plunging around around 15%.
Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. As of midmorning trading, Brent and U.S. crude oil rose 2%.
U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were slightly lower.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1,250 points. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 7%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025.
Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months.
Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines.
Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 5%.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
articles.title_zh: Nvidia has lost nearly $1.4 trillion since its October record
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is on track for its fifth straight losing week, and the slide since its October record has now erased nearly $1.4 trillion in market value.
Thursday did a lot of the damage. At its morning low, Nvidia was down more than 9%, knocking nearly $450 billion off its market value in a matter of hours and leaving the company worth about $4.4 trillion. A close there would be the stock's worst day since the DeepSeek sell-off in January 2025.
Nvidia has plenty of company.
AMD ( AMD ), Micron ( MU ), and Arm ( ARM ) are posting steep double-digit losses, and Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ) are falling near 10%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) is now more than a third below its June record.
Nvidia itself is down nearly 25% from its Oct. 6 record close and trading below its 200-day moving average .
The trigger this time is Washington. Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and candidates in both parties campaigned against AI data centers , the buildings that run on Nvidia's chips. The Senate came close to passing a bill this fall that would have made data centers pay more of the power costs they create.
Losing streaks this long don't come often for Nvidia. Since its 1999 IPO, the stock has strung together five or more down weeks just 12 times before this one. The longest ran seven weeks, in the summer of 2008.
The last one is the streak bulls will want to remember. It ended in October 2022, about a month before ChatGPT's launch set off the AI boom, and Nvidia's stock roughly quadrupled over the following year.
That's the best case, not the base case. Nvidia was higher 13 weeks later in only five of the 12 earlier streaks, though it was up a year later in eight. The worst came in 2002, when the stock lost nearly two-thirds of its value over the following year.
For now, Washington is the new worry hanging over the stock.
"There will be congressional hearings," Stifel's Brian Gardner told Reuters ahead of the vote. "There will be investigations."

articles.title_orig: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
articles.title_zh: Tankers hit in Hormuz as Iran keeps up pressure after US vote
articles.content_orig:
At least five tankers have been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian forces said, making clear that shipping would remain in peril as long as the United States and Israel’s war on the country is unresolved.
Since the war on Iran began in late February, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.
“Last night … a large oil tanker attempting to pass through the illegal passageway south of the Strait of Hormuz suffered a fire after striking a mine and was brought to a halt,” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) told the Fars news agency on Thursday.
“Another supertanker was halted by a massive fire while exiting the eastern Strait of Hormuz. A tugboat that had approached the supertanker to extinguish the fire also caught fire,” the IRGC added.
The Iranian army later said three more tankers were hit by naval mines and caught fire.
“Early this morning, a violating oil tanker – navigating through an unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz – caught fire and came to a halt after striking a naval mine,” the army said, according to the official IRNA news agency.
“Today at around noon, two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in the unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz,” said another army statement carried by IRNA.
Separately, the British military said a tanker was struck by two projectiles off Qatar’s coast.
The vessel was hit about 50 nautical miles (about 93 kilometres) north of Qatar’s ⁠Madinat ash-Shamal on Wednesday at 23:20 GMT, the ⁠United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Thursday.
UKMTO did not identify the tanker or which country’s flag it was sailing under. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack.
In an incident last week, a Qatari tanker was hit by “unidentified objects” while sailing in the Gulf.
The liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Mayeda was hit on October 30, the Qatar Gas Transport Company (Nakilat) said on Sunday.
No crew members were injured, and there ‌was no environmental impact, the company said, adding that the vessel remained ‌safe and ‌operational while the impact was being assessed.
Attacks on tankers in the Gulf are still running close to a record pace.
UKMTO said in a report last month that it was “struggling to accurately report” the true number of attacks as the majority of ships now refuse to report them.
Qatar has stepped up mediation efforts to resume talks on ending the war in recent days.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ spokesperson said on Tuesday that ⁠both sides were reviewing proposals ⁠put forward by mediators, with talks continuing.
But unnamed Pentagon officials and military commanders told The New York Times on Wednesday that thousands of US air and naval forces on more than a dozen ships and at bases around the Middle East and in the US are poised to resume major combat operations against Iran on President Donald Trump’s orders.
Iranian government and military leaders, however, have warned of repercussions if the US or Israel pursue further military action.
On Wednesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US, which he said would remain hostile towards Iran no matter which party was in power.
IRGC Ground Force commander Brigadier General Mohammad Karami said on Wednesday that the continuation of “hostile and brutal actions by Iran’s enemies” would lead to “further Iranian victories and greater national pride”, while accelerating the expulsion of foreign powers from the region and the collapse of Israel.

articles.title_orig: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
articles.title_zh: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
articles.content_orig:
Shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX have plunged as tech and artificial intelligence stocks more broadly plummeted a day after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterms.
Those losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index down, which had fallen by more than 5% at one point in early trading.
The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the artificial intelligence (AI) industry following Democrat wins in key data centre states including Texas.
Following the election, some tech leaders have acknowledged they need to improve their communication around data centres and the benefits of AI.
SpaceX shares were down more than 9% in by lunchtime in Thursday trading, while Tesla shares dropped more than 11%.
Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in chipmakers have been suffering, with AMD dropping more than 14% on Thursday, while Micron shares had dropped by as much as 17% before recovering slightly.
Intel shares are down by more than 7% and shares in Nvidia have fallen nearly 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen by 10%.
The stock falls also hit the S&P 500 index, which dropped by 3.8% by lunchtime.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.
"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.
"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick agreed that the industry needed to improve their communication about the benefits of AI.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction .

articles.title_orig: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.title_zh: Joint List says it will back Eisenkot to form Israel’s next government
articles.content_orig:
The Joint List alliance of Arab-led parties says it will back Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a new government after last week’s election.
“The Joint List announced today, Thursday, that it will inform the President of the State, Isaac Herzog, this evening of its decision to recommend that Gadi Eisenkot be tasked with forming the government,” the alliance said in a statement.
Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament in last week’s general election, a result that could give them significant influence over the formation of the next government.
Once the Joint List’s 11 lawmakers formally submit their recommendation, Eisenkot is expected to have the backing of 67 lawmakers, exceeding the 61-seat majority threshold in the Knesset.
Earlier, Ra’am, an Arab-led party with eight seats, said it would also recommend Eisenkot.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc with 53 seats may not yield 53 endorsements, as Degel HaTorah, which holds four of United Torah Judaism’s seven seats, said it would recommend neither candidate.
The ultra-Orthodox faction broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting Haredi men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.
Netanyahu has also claimed repeatedly and without evidence that Arab parties committed fraud during the elections with foreign backing.
The prime minister and his Likud party have cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists who allegedly bribed voters before polls opened. They are suspected of connections with the Ra’am party, although the party denies any involvement.
Netanyahu and Likud also suggested that the opposition bloc joining with Arab-led parties would be treasonous. In a statement after the vote, Likud warned that Zionist parties cooperating with the Arab bloc would be “dangerous to Israel”.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee certified the results of the election on Wednesday after finding no evidence of fraud.
President Herzog has also accepted the results and begun consultations with party leaders on whom to task with forming the next government.
He also backed investigating suspected interference but warned against smearing voters who are Palestinian citizens of Israel, saying he had “great respect” for the country’s Palestinian minority, which makes up about 20 percent of the population.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said.
On Wednesday, the president said he had met representatives of the Religious Zionism and Zehut, Shas and Yisrael Beytenu factions.
In a post on X, Herzog said he “received their recommendations regarding the identity of the Knesset member upon whom the task of forming the government should be assigned”.
Herzog added that talks would also continue on Thursday.
Once the consultations end, Herzog will choose the candidate he considers best placed to assemble a coalition, almost certainly Netanyahu or Eisenkot. He has several days to announce his decision, after which the nominee will have 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
If neither man succeeds, Israel would hold another election early next year.
Reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said that if Eisenkot is able to form a government, then he will become Israel’s next prime minister and Netanyahu will likely be the head of the opposition.
“It is up to Gadi Eisenkot to do what he promised, to oust Benjamin Netanyahu. And to do that, he needs to have 61 votes in the Knesset, which means that he needs the votes of the Palestinian-Israeli parties, parties that he does not want to partner up with,” she said.
“But he will most likely have to reach some sort of deal, for [the Palestinian-Israeli parties] to abstain at the very least, to make sure that his government is sworn in and a new chapter in Israeli politics is able to begin,” she added.

articles.title_orig: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.title_zh: ‘I worry people will forget Hong Kong’: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive: pro-democracy activist’s prison letters reveal fascination with AI, brushes with Triads and an appetite for books
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
F rom inside Hong Kong’s oldest maximum security prison, where he swaps books with Triad gang members and studies law, Joshua Wong writes letters like a man desperate to stay connected to the outside world.
Excerpts from his private prison writings reveal the pro-democracy activist asking friends to take screenshots of social media accounts and put questions to AI chatbots on his behalf.
To one acquaintance, he writes about his prison reading habits. “Some of the old-school triad bosses in here have also lent me books,” he says in the letters to friends, seen exclusively by the Guardian. “They read too. One of them lent me Mario Puzo’s The Godfather (lol).”
The 30-year-old Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s now-squashed democracy movement, has been imprisoned since November 2020.
On Thursday, he was sentenced to 10 years for foreign collusion , his second conviction under the national security law imposed by Beijing in 2020. Wong pleaded guilty to the charge in September.
Wong is the only pro-democracy activist to be prosecuted twice under the national security legislation. He had been due to be released in January, before the latest prosecution, and will now serve his two sentences concurrently.
Despite spending his 21st, 25th and 30th birthdays in prison, Wong’s letters – written between August and October – show his resolve and continuing concern about Hong Kong’s future.
“The only thing I worry about is that people will forget Hong Kong, and that amid competition and struggles between great powers, they will forget the countless ordinary, unknown people in different places who have paid a price for their beliefs,” he writes.
In Stanley prison, where young inmates use M&Ms as currency, he spends time exercising, learning to play the guitar and teaching English to other prisoners.
“I was teaching English to a Russian,” he says in one letter. “When he asked me what the word ‘totalitarian’ meant, I simply answered, ‘Putin’ (lol)”.
Books appear to be central to his life. His reading list includes Patriot, the memoir of Russian opposition leader, Alexei Navalny, who died in prison in 2024; biographies of Steve Jobs, Nelson Mandela, Benjamin Franklin; and the memoir of former Citibank trader turned YouTuber and inequality campaigner, Gary Stevenson.
On the day of the US presidential election in November 2024, he watched votes come in while holding a copy of JD Vance’s bestselling memoir, Hillbilly Elegy.
Wong gained international attention during the 2014 Umbrella protests , which paralysed the city’s financial centre and galvanised a generation of young people. In October 2014, he appeared – with his trademark black-rimmed spectacles – on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the protests and immediately took to the streets.
In 2020, Beijing said its introduction of the national security law was needed to restore stability to the former British colony, but critics said it gave authorities sweeping powers to crack down on free speech and dissent.
Since then, activists and journalists have been arrested, independent newsrooms closed, and much of the city’s political opposition forced into exile . There have been more than 400 arrests under national security legislation, according to Hong Kong’s security bureau.
“Joshua’s case is part of an attempt to control how my generation’s political history is remembered,” says Frances Hui, a childhood friend and pro-democracy activist in exile.
“For years, people around the world could hear him argue, organise, and explain what he thought Hong Kong’s future should be. Now we can barely hear from him at all.”
In his letters, Wong says Mandela inspired him to study law and he has enrolled in an undergraduate company law course.
He says that he has lost weight, but has a strict routine of pull-ups, squats and pushups. He also reads the Bible and recites passages from the book of Joshua and the Corinthians.
Wong’s childhood friends and fellow activists say the Hong Kong they once fought for no longer exists.
“It is hard to say whose side time is on,” says another childhood friend, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.
Hui says that Hong Kong authorities had waited nearly five years after the alleged crime to prosecute Wong – just before his release.
“By the time he sees freedom, he is most certainly not going to be the young boy we once remembered,” she says.

articles.title_orig: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.title_zh: After Riots and Protests, French Workers Are Going on Strike
articles.content_orig:
• General strike : French riot police have fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon while scuffles have broken out in Nantes and authorities have arrested agitators who vandalized a Rennes hotel. But overall, the roughly 200 demonstrations across France on Thursday – attended by almost 600,000 people – have remained relatively peaceful.
• Widespread disruptions : The strike is organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions. Education, health care, public transportation and other sectors have been impacted with many services closed for the day.
• Europe discontent : Anti-government protests have swept across the continent in recent weeks. In Greece , students and teachers gathered in central Athens on Thursday to stress the importance of free public education and protest the rising housing and food costs affecting students.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “social conference” with employers and unions next Monday as hundreds of thousands of people participate in protests across the country.
The conference will be aimed at addressing questions around “purchasing power and wages,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement .
Today’s general strike and protests have been organized by L’intersyndicale, the group that represents all of France’s main trade unions.
Place de la Nation, in eastern Paris, is a historic plaza synonymous with protest. Marches often end here, and we’re used to seeing huge clouds of tear gas as protesters clash with police.
But tonight, it’s quite an unusual and arresting sight to see the square so full after dark. A huge mass of people continue to stand still beneath a monument celebrating the triumph of the French Republic.
The protest in Paris was authorized by city officials to wrap up at 7 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET). But with less than 30 minutes to go, it’s unlikely everyone will be able to disperse quickly.
Although this movement initially began with students protesting the state of the education system, it has morphed into one that includes several other concerns united by a key factor: the poor state of the economy.
Protesters on Thursday said they are anxious about low salaries, which have not kept up with inflation, as well as underresourced public services.
“There is a lot of concern about the future, notably the issues of salaries, public services,” Alice Martinovic, an 18-year-old student participating in the Paris protest, told Reuters.
“I hope in the upcoming elections the candidates will really think about this movement and include the opinions of young people, of students, who are now joined by a lot of other workers.”
Meanwhile, Mehdi Dumontroty, a 45-year-old firefighter also protesting in Paris, told Reuters that “our pay has not kept up with inflation.”
“What happened this summer proves that we were right when we said we needed more resources to deal with the crisis that we faced,” he said, referencing fierce wildfires which swept across southern France amid record-breaking, climate change-fueled heat waves.
Almost 600,000 protesters are on the streets of France today, the country’s interior ministry has just estimated, making Thursday the biggest day of protests since this current wave of unrest began in September.
Earlier today, at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET), the ministry had estimated that 270,000 people were protesting but that number excluded Paris, where a march began this afternoon.
The ministry is expected to release its final figures later today but, as of now, its current estimates indicate that these demonstrations are not quite as big as the 2023 pension reform protests.
French education minister Édouard Geffray has condemned what he said was a “deliberate act of arson” at a school near the city of Toulouse in southern France.
The minister thanked firefighters and law enforcement officials for helping to “limit the damage” cause by the flames.
“This deliberate act of arson could have had tragic consequences for human life. I condemn it in the strongest possible terms and call on everyone to condemn it unequivocally,” he added, while vowing to hold those responsible to account.
Earlier, France’s interior ministry said the blaze started after fireworks were directed at an office hosting the school’s student services.
Authorities in Rennes said they arrested “several dozen” masked individuals who vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” union members who were protesting earlier today.
Photos taken by local media show that vandals smashed the hotel’s glass doors and painted graffiti on windows.
Some masked individuals also tried to erect barricades to block some of the city’s roads, lit fires in garbage bins, and threw heavy pétanque balls – used in a popular French game – at police, authorities added.
Despite violent clashes like this, however, the protests today have largely been peaceful even as they have been attended by hundreds of thousands of people.
As today’s march in Paris got underway, the trade unions were in a jubilant mood. Music blared out as the crowd, dominated by left-wing groups, sang and chanted slogans against the government and the far-right.
A police helicopter buzzed above, but in the confines of the avenue we were walking down, there was little sense of the heavy police presence around the protest.
In the distance, the soaring statue of Marianne – the national symbol of France – got smaller and smaller as the march inched its way forward.
The protest route is packed. The movement of the crowd has been brought to a near standstill at points by the sheer quantity of people.
Later, several protesters were seen lying on the ground being treated by street medics, with blood flowing from the head of an older man. A bystander said the man was struck by police, but an officer at the scene said they were unaware of any incident.
At one point, protesters scattered as tear gas was deployed by police, followed by mass cries of “everyone hates the police.”
The mood of the crowd has lost its upbeat feel.
Several of France’s biggest unions, representing everyone from students, teachers and postal workers to doctors, pharmacists and transport workers, have called for a nationwide strike. So, how is that affecting these essential services?
Schools: About 13% of all school staff are participating in the strikes, France’s education ministry estimates, including 16% of all teachers. Around 19% of schools and 18% of colleges across France are affected by the strike.
Universities: About one in three of France’s higher education are “disrupted” because of the strikes and protests, the government told CNN.
Hospitals: Very few public hospital staff – only about 4% of the workforce – are participating in the strike, France’s healthcare ministry told CNN. “No significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported,” the ministry added. Two of France’s main unions representing both public and private healthcare workers had called on them to strike, citing the high cost of living and the deterioriation of public services.
Transport: Four in 10 of today’s scheduled trains have been canceled, though a handful of those cancelations are due to other factors like unavailable equipment, according to tracking website Trayn.
The labor unions that have called today’s demonstrations in France are demanding higher wages and pensions. In particular, the largest of the unions – the CGT – says the minimum wage needs to be increased immediately by 10%.
Last month, the CGT claimed there had been a big increase in the number of professions paying some employees less than the minimum wage. Another union - the CFDT – is demanding a 100 euro increase in the minimum monthly wage, about 7%.
Maud Millier, a CGT official in Lyon, said that the government’s announced minimum wage increase, from November 1, amounts to just €15 for someone earning the minimum wage, which she said was nowhere near enough given rising fuel and food pr

articles.title_orig: Thousands of troops secure Indonesia trial as tensions run high over wiretap scandal
articles.title_zh: Thousands of troops secure Indonesia trial as tensions run high over wiretap scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jakarta. The government has acknowledged that electronic devices could be used to illegally intercept President Prabowo Subianto's communications despite layers of security protecting the head of state, as police investigate allegations involving three senior officers.
State Secretary Minister Prasetyo Hadi said on Wednesday that the government had put various security measures in place to protect the president, but these could not entirely rule out the possibility of unauthorized access to his electronic communications.
“Even so, there are individuals who could exploit the technical possibilities offered by electronic equipment,” Prasetyo told reporters at the Presidential Palace in Jakarta.
The National Police's (Polri) Criminal Investigation Department named former presidential chief of staff and former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo a suspect on Tuesday in a case involving alleged illegal wiretapping, unauthorized access and deletion of electronic data.
Two active police generals, Inspector General Ahrie Sonta and Inspector General Eko Hadi, were also named suspects. Another individual is being questioned as a witness.
The three suspects are alleged to have used a Lawful Interception Management System (LIMS), a platform that manages the interception of communications through telecommunications networks.
LIMS is designed to handle interception requests, register targets, manage authorization, and distribute intercepted information to legally authorized institutions. Unlike spyware applications that require access to a target's device, the system can obtain communications through infrastructure operated by telecommunications providers, subject to legal requirements and authorization.
Prasetyo said he could not yet confirm which conversations had allegedly been intercepted by the three officers.
He urged the public to wait for the outcome of the police investigation before drawing conclusions, including about the communications targeted, the alleged motive and who may have received the intercepted information.
Government Reviews Wiretapping Rules
Separately, Coordinating Minister for Law, Human Rights, Immigration, and Corrections Yusril Ihza Mahendra said the government would review regulations governing wiretapping following the allegations involving senior police officers.
Yusril said the review would involve coordination with the Coordinating Ministry for Political and Security Affairs and relevant institutions, including the National Cyber and Crypto Agency (BSSN).
“Of course, we will conduct an evaluation,” Yusril told reporters in Jakarta on Tuesday.
He said several state institutions were legally authorized to conduct wiretapping using specialized equipment, including the National Narcotics Agency (BNN), the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK), the Attorney General's Office and the National Police.
However, such operations must comply with applicable laws and procedures. Yusril said the police, for example, had internal regulations governing how wiretapping could be conducted.
He warned that unauthorized interception or surveillance carried out for purposes unrelated to an institution's official duties could constitute a criminal offense, punishable under the Criminal Code or the Electronic Information and Transactions Law.

articles.title_orig: AI stocks are in free-fall as investors panic over the risk of a data center slowdown
articles.title_zh: AI stocks are in free-fall as investors panic over the risk of a data center slowdown
articles.content_orig:
Investors' postelection euphoria lasted just one day before fears about the AI trade came roaring into view.
Democrats' sweeping victories on Tuesday sparked a monster postelection rally , but US stocks are now getting pummeled by worries that the blue wave will usher in a new era of tighter regulation for data centers and AI development, with cascading effects for the bull market and broader economic growth.
Here's where major indexes stood around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday:
At the forefront of investors' anxieties is the idea that newly elected Democrats at the state and federal level will tighten the reins on data center construction, slowing AI capex at a time when investment spending is still powering a significant portion of economic growth and the yearslong bull market in tech stocks.
AI stocks plummeted on Thursday, extending yesterday's declines for infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and chip makers like Nvidia. But whereas some AI-linked names such as hyperscalers gained in Wednesday's session, the rout on Thursday battered the AI trade broadly.
The most painful losses were in neoclouds, memory and chip stocks, and data center operators.
All three benchmark indexes tumbled into the red, on track for their worst trading day since the Liberation Day stock crash in 2025. The Dow, which logged its best day on Wednesday since April 2025, dropped more than 1,300 points, while the Nasdaq 100 plunged 5%.
The tech-heavy index is now down 13% from its latest high and officially in a correction. It dropped below its 200-day moving average during the session, breaching a closely watched technical support level.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Here were the most notable moves in the tech sector:
Thursday's decline erased most of the gains logged on Wednesday, when investors piled into hyperscalers on optimism that AI capex will slow, which would be a positive for these companies' financials. The logic today, though, seems to be driven by a broader risk-off move, with investors looking to reduce exposure to the AI sector amid data center uncertainty. Traders have also been eager to take profits lately, punishing various hyperscalers after quarterly earnings even when firms beat on the bottom line and signaled greater spending discipline heading into 2027.
"There's blood on the streets today as AI-linked names tumble," Nick Puckrin, a cross-asset analyst, wrote in a note. "The midterm election result didn't really create a new fear, it was just the gust of wind that pushed over the house of cards that was already getting shaky."
In a note, analysts at Jefferies called Democratic Sweep a "Worst-Case Near-Term Scenario" for the AI trade, pointing to the potential for tighter data center regulation . The firm also revised its outlook for data center capacity through the end of the decade downward.
Meta President Dina Powell McCormick also flagged greater difficulties firms would face going forward to build new data centers, adding to investor anxiety.
"What I mean by that is to start new data center build-outs today in the United States will be very challenging," McCormick said, speaking at the Wall Street Journal Tech conference in California on Wednesday. Meta has emerged as one of the largest players in the data center space, with construction on its $50 billion Hyperion data center in Louisiana and its $14 billion Texas data center underway.
Investors are also wrestling with anxiety about what will happen to the US economy and bull market if investment slows. The market has been increasingly aware that AI is accounting for a growing share of US growth. Data center construction, for instance, was one of the only areas of construction spending that grew in September, soaring 80% while spending in most other sectors declined, according to an analysis from Harvard economist Jason Furman.
"Will the shift in Congress actually slow tech down? If yes (as many assume, though I'm less sure), can the rest of the market and economy thrive without the shield of tech earnings and spending?" top economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on LinkedIn.
The AI infrastructure space appears to be facing a "reality check," top economist David Rosenberg wrote in a note to clients on Thursday.
"The question becomes the economic impact as we see, at the least, a pause in the data center construction mania," he added.
It's been a volatile week for markets , with investors also slogging through Big Tech earnings and key economic data releases. All eyes will be on the October jobs report coming out Friday, which is expected to shape the Fed's path for future rate hikes heading into 2027.

articles.title_orig: China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and GCSA Jointly Establish the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research
articles.title_zh: China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and GCSA Jointly Establish the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG , Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- China Resources Longdation's Aethereal Cybersecurity and Global Cybersecurity Alliance Limited (GCSA) have announced the joint establishment of the Centre for AI and Cybersecurity Research. The initiative brings together both parties' technological expertise and industry resources in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and industrial applications to advance research, product innovation, and industry collaboration.
Founded in 1982, China Resources Longdation operates across property management, asset management, and community services. Its Aethereal Cybersecurity business specializes in AI-driven digital transformation and cybersecurity services for government agencies and enterprises, providing professional technologies and solutions to Hong Kong SAR 's government departments, public institutions, and businesses, supported by relevant cybersecurity qualifications. GCSA is committed to advancing technological innovation, research collaboration, and international exchange in cybersecurity, with a particular focus on emerging security challenges involving AI, Web3, and digital finance.
The two parties will strengthen their cooperation in cybersecurity. The Centre will focus on joint research and development in AI-powered fraud prevention, cyber threat detection, digital financial security, and cybersecurity automation. Key areas of exploration include AI deception honeypots, intelligent fraud detection, threat intelligence analysis, and security platforms, with an emphasis on practical applications.
By combining their respective resources and professional service capabilities, the partnership aims to foster cross-organizational collaboration in AI and cybersecurity, contributing to the development of the digital economy and cybersecurity industry.
Contact: Laber Mann, media@gcsa.com

articles.title_orig: Sony revives the Walkman’s iconic MDR-3 headphones with USB-C for $60
articles.title_zh: Sony revives the Walkman’s iconic MDR-3 headphones with USB-C for $60
articles.content_orig:
Sony is bringing back its iconic Walkman MDR-3 headphones for the modern era with a USB-C connection and a price tag of $60.
Originally launched in 1979, Sony’s MDR-3 headphone lineup served as a companion to the Walkman cassette player and, now, they’re making a comeback. The Sony MDR-3R headphones are a USB-C revival of the classic design, just with connectivity that actually works on modern devices.
The design, Sony says, is a “faithful recreation” of the original and comes with blue or orange ear pads. Even the packaging and included manual “inherit the design of the original model.” As for the actual sound quality, Sony has “re-engineered” the same 23mm driver with sound “close to the original,” though refined for modern sound.
Along with the USB-C connection, they also feature a microphone and in-line remote, and Sony incorporated recycled plastic too.
Sony MDR-3R are available starting today for $59.99 from typical retailers.
Celebrating the Walkman’s role in Netflix’s Stranger Things, Sony is also releasing a red/black variant to match the ones worn by Max in the show. Those will cost $79.99.

articles.title_orig: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
articles.title_zh: Marc Lore's Wonder confidentially files for IPO
articles.content_orig:
Food startup Wonder has confidentially filed for an initial public offering, the company said Thursday.
Created by serial entrepreneur Marc Lore in 2018, Wonder advertises itself as "the best restaurants from across the country, all in one place," available for delivery and takeout on its vertically integrated app.
Originally envisioned as a new take on food delivery through sprinter vans outfitted with mobile kitchens, Wonder has grown to roughly 170 brick-and-mortar locations throughout the U.S. Its locations serve menu items from more than two dozen "restaurants" across a variety of cuisines, some with branding from celebrity chefs.
Starting Nov. 17, the company plans to introduce more dining options through Wonder Create. Influencers, entrepreneurs and brands can pay $10 a month to start their own restaurant business based out of a Wonder location and earn a portion of the revenue from orders.
Wonder has spent at least $1 billion on acquisitions, such as delivery service Grubhub, meal kit brand Blue Apron and delivery and logistics provider Relay, along with some buzzy restaurant concepts. Wonder has been able to afford such expensive dealmaking thanks to more than $3 billion in venture funding.
Wonder's Series D fundraising round earlier this year raised its pre-money valuation to $9 billion.
With the proceeds from an IPO, Wonder will be able to make more acquisitions and work toward its goal of making food more accessible, Lore told CNBC in September.
But as a public company, Wonder will also likely face investor scrutiny. Weak consumer sentiment has weighed on restaurant stocks recently, plus market volatility has resulted in a shaky IPO market for companies across a range of industries.
Lore previously founded Diapers.com and Jet.com, which he sold to Amazon and Walmart, respectively.

articles.title_orig: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.title_zh: Clashes erupt in France as ‘Black Thursday’ protests sweep the nation
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — Riot police clashed with protesters in Lyon on Thursday as a nationwide public sector strike tapped into growing anger over deteriorating services and the rising cost of living.
Paris’ iconic Eiffel Tower was closed because of the strike.
Officers clad in black helmets and protective clothing charged at crowds in Lyon after the demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of the high school protest movement turned violent and fires were set in the streets. Water cannons were also deployed. Some of the protesters wore gas masks and safety glasses as a precaution against tear gas.
Images from Paris showed students and other protesters facing off against riot police.
Police were “keeping the situation under control, but it remains tense,” the French Interior Ministry said in a statement at 1 p.m. local time (7 a.m. ET).
“Several violent acts have been committed as part of the high school student movement,” the statement said. After fireworks were fired at a school near the southern city of Toulouse, a fire broke out “that burned the student services office,” it added.
In the city of Rennes in northwest France, metal pétanque balls were thrown at officers, the statement said, adding that police had been pelted with other projectiles in the cities of Pau and Orleans.
Around 250 rallies against rising living costs had been planned in cities and towns across the country and hundreds of thousands of people would likely turn out, unions said before the events kicked off.
France’s main unions, including the CGT and CNT representing public and private sector workers, and the UNEF, representing students, warned the government of President Emmanuel Macron’s that the country was on the brink or recession.
“Everything is going up except wages and pensions,” they said in a joint statement. “Anger is immense.”
“The situation in this country is fragile. The pressing social and environmental challenges must be addressed without delay,” the statement added.
The movement grew from a student protest over staff shortages at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris. Videos of the blockade spread on social media, and soon protests expanded to high schools across the nation.
As the movement grew, the list of grievances expanded beyond the failings of the public school system to encompass broader economic, political and social dissatisfaction. Soon, university students, teachers, parents and politicians also joined.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters have since taken to the streets as the demonstrations expanded, with participants holding signs criticizing the far-right National Rally party and warning of the risks of climate change and artificial intelligence. A multitude of Palestinian flags have also been seen.
Macron, who will leave office in May, convened a defense ‌and security meeting Wednesday ahead of the protests. Later, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that 70,000 police officers would be deployed Thursday, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters.
Police have previously been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics. Last month, a 15-year-old was maimed by a sting ball grenade fired by police and a 14-year-old suffered a jaw fracture in a similar incident.
Several other have also suffered life-changing injuries and a 59-year-old man, identified as Christophe M, died Oct. 17 of “a critical cardio-respiratory failing” after leaving Paris’ Place de la République which had been tear-gassed be police. An investigation into his death is ongoing.
Zacharie Petit reported from Paris and Henry Austin from London.
Zacharie Petit is a producer in Paris.
Henry Austin is a senior editor for NBC News Digital based in London.

articles.title_orig: Bad News for Italian Chef Who Balked at Pineapple Pizza
articles.title_zh: Bad News for Italian Chef Who Balked at Pineapple Pizza
articles.content_orig:
An Italian chef sacked from a Brisbane restaurant had refused to put pineapple on a pizza because it was an "insult to his culture".
Davide Tamburella was fired from the now-closed La Costa restaurant in May, a fortnight after a meeting with management who had a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function. At the time, the chef had stated that any direction from management "need not be followed when it is offensive to his culture".
The details came to light after the chef went to Australia's Fair Work Commission claiming he had been unfairly dismissed.
In its ruling released on Tuesday, the commission noted that Tamburella's refusal to put pineapple on the pizzas was because "he considers, as an Italian, that putting pineapple on a pizza is an insult to his culture".
It also noted that it was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
He had previously requested his boss to "check how important it is for Italians not to put pineapple on a pizza".
The state of Queensland, where the restaurant is located, is considered Australia's pineapple heartland and produces all of the country's commercially-grown pineapples.
On the Sunshine Coast, visitors regularly stop to take photos next to The Big Pineapple, a heritage-listed 16m-tall fibreglass model of the fruit, which has become a local landmark.
Other concerns were raised about Tamburella using foul language, his communication style and "escalation of frustration in the workplace".
The ruling also detailed an incident at work in April this year where Tamburella fractured bones in his right hand when he struck a metal hand rail.
Tamburella had been hoping the restaurant would sponsor a visa for him that allows skilled workers to be permanent residents.
However after his sacking, the restaurant ended that  process, the tribunal heard.
He lost his unfair dismissal claim on the grounds that the application had been filed too late, according to the ruling.
The restaurant's managing director, Elliot Ingram, told the Daily Mail there was "more to this story than a pizza topping".
The BBC has approached Tamburella for comment.
On the chef's LinkedIn profile, he describes himself as someone who, throughout his career, has focused on "delivering exceptional food" and "improving business performance".
Three months ago he posted a "letter for chefs" with the theme "respecting the ingredients".
The LinkedIn profile states he now works at another Brisbane restaurant. A BBC check has found that pineapple is not on its menu.

articles.title_orig: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.title_zh: Record share of first-time homebuyers paying in cash as Great Wealth Transfer picks up steam
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Great Wealth Transfer is starting to impact the housing market.
A record share of first-time homebuyers are paying for their properties in cash, a sign that more buyers are likely using money they inherited from older generations to help fund their purchases.
Last year, 1 in 10 first-time buyers did an all-cash transaction, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors, the fourth straight year with an increase, and the largest share since the trade group began collecting data on those transactions in 2003. Among first-time all-cash buyers, 28% reported using an inheritance to help fund their deal, compared with just 9% of first-time buyers who financed.
As home prices hover near all-time highs and mortgage rates stay north of 7% , pricing out many prospective buyers, some portion of those buyers may simply be waiting for an inheritance or other significant help from wealthy baby boomers or members of the Silent Generation.
"It is critical when analyzing first-time buyers to understand there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth," the report said.
Buyers reliant on wealth transfers look different from those who finance and use their own savings. As modern life expectancy increases, delaying inheritances, first-time all-cash buyers are typically deep into middle age. The median first-time buyer paying all cash is 54 years old, according to the report, significantly older than the median age of 38 for first-time buyers financing their homes.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

articles.title_orig: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.title_zh: Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger found dead in Berlin hotel
articles.content_orig:
Bavarian politician Hubert Aiwanger was found dead in a hotel in Berlin on Wednesday, the German capital's public prosecutor's office said.
Aiwanger was Bavaria's deputy premier, economy minister and the chairman of the right-wing populist Free Voters party. He was 55 years old.
The circumstances surrounding Aiwanger's death are still unclear. Police and prosecutors in the German capital have launched an investigation.
On Wednesday evening, investigators said the goal is to "determine the specific cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it, as well as to rule out any possible foul play."
Aiwanger had been feeling unwell on Wednesday, German tabloid Bild reported.
He was scheduled to deliver a speech at the opening of a party office in Berlin but canceled his appearance for health reasons, German news agency dpa reported.
Aiwanger's body was found on Wednesday evening at the "Neuer Fritz" Hotel on Friedrichstrasse in Berlin-Mitte, according to Bild .
Bavarian state premier, the Christian Social Union 's Markus Söder, has said he is "deeply shocked" by the news of his deputy's death.
"The sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy," Söder said in a post on X.
"Our thoughts are now first and foremost with his family and his children. We mourn with them and pray for them."
Born in Lower Bavaria in southern Germany , Aiwanger was elected to the Bavarian State Parliament in 2008 with the Free Voters and became their parliamentary group leader.
Since 2018, his party has been in a coalition with the center-right CSU, the Bavarian sister party of the ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) . Aiwanger served as the state's Minister of Economic Affairs and deputy premier.
Aiwanger was the face of the Free Voters in Bavaria and across Germany, and was known for his combative approach.
But his political success in the state did not translate to the national level, as the Free Voters never won enough seats to enter the Bundestag , Germany's federal parliament.
In the weeks before state elections in 2023, Aiwanger became embroiled in a national scandal when the Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that he had written an antisemitic leaflet during high school in the 1980s, which included references to Nazi-era atrocities such as Auschwitz.
He is survived by two children. He was not married but lived with Tanja Schweiger, a district administrator for the Free Voters.

articles.title_orig: Mother, daughter found dead after suspected grizzly attack
articles.title_zh: Mother, daughter found dead after suspected grizzly attack
articles.content_orig:
A mother and daughter have died after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the Canadian province of British Columbia, their family has announced.
The women - identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20 -were reported missing on 1 November when they did not return from what was supposed to be a short afternoon walk, the family said.
Their remains were found in a trail area in Bella Coola, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS), which said evidence at the scene "suggested an animal may have been involved".
Conservation officers are working to track down any bears involved.
Balcarras' remains were found on Monday and Reed's on Tuesday during search efforts by conservation officers and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP).
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the BCCOS, said it was not yet clear if more than one was potentially involved in the women's deaths.
He added that any captured bear would be assessed and if it is found to have been involved in the attack "it will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh Balcarras, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Balcarras had recently moved to Bella Coola to pursue a new career and begin a new chapter in her life, according to an online fundraiser to help the family with funeral costs.
Grizzly bears are listed as a species of "special concern" under federal legislation, and are an important part of the British Columbia landscape, according to Environmental Reporting BC .
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in the province, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, which has classified them as vulnerable.
According to the ministry, conflicts between bears and humans are "relatively rare" unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs and food.
But there have been a number of attacks in British Columbia in recent years.
A grizzly bear injured two hikers in the McGregor Mountain area in October 2025, one of whom died later due to critical injuries. The bear was later found dead.
The following month, a bear attacked a school group - also in the Bella Coola area - injuring 11 people.
The BC Wildlife Federation (BCWF) has said that reports of grizzly-human conflicts have risen since the province introduced a ban on hunting grizzly bears for sport in 2017.
"With no hunting pressure, grizzlies and humans will increasingly occupy the same spaces with inevitable consequences," the BCWF's executive director Jesse Zeman said at the time.

articles.title_orig: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.title_zh: AI backlash threatens trillion-dollar data centre boom, say tech leaders
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

articles.title_orig: Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Midterm Sweep
articles.title_zh: Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Midterm Sweep
articles.content_orig:
Wall Street may not be thrilled with Tuesday night’s blue tsunami , but many top executives see a more fundamental problem that’s threatening US business: a two-party system that’s increasingly dominated by extremism on both sides, On The Money has learned.
The Democrats gave the GOP a thumping whose decisiveness surprised many pundits — easily taking control of both the House and Senate with left wingers picking up important seats in both chambers.
Far-left members of the Democratic Socialists of America won key races. James Talarico, known for his belief in six genders, won in Texas. A Democrat took a Senate seat in deep-red South Carolina and a man who campaigned with the noxious Hasan Piker won in Michigan.
These are the types of pols who hate Israel, would love to bring back trans day of visibility on Easter Sunday and would like nothing less than criminalizing making money even if there’s no criminality involved.
Yet, the CEOs I speak to say if the GOP pulled out a semblance of a victory (like keeping the Senate) whatever happened wasn’t going to be good because this should have been a lay-up election for the GOP given the top-line economic numbers. Even worse, they don’t see the GOP pulling away from the intense populism of the Trump agenda, and that goes to the heart of their angst.
For one, they’re not holding their breath for an end to Trump’s bizarre habit of picking candidates that show only obsequiousness to MAGA, despite their unelectability (think Ken Paxton). Nor do they see him backing off tariffs.
That’s despite the damage tariffs did to the GOP in the midterms – not to mention consumers’ wallets. Ditto for immigration enforcement that went beyond sending criminals back to wherever they came from and which now makes it harder to find workers.
The war with Iran won’t be concluded for some time because Trump can’t decide whether to fully embrace the hawks in his administration or those wanting an immediate negotiated peace. That means its impact on gas prices will remain.
Moreover, the GOP won’t be going back to its more corporatist roots, where leaders focused on tax and regulation cuts and supported free trade.
“MAGA is now 40% of Republican primary voters, and the DSA-types 35% of Democratic Party voters,” said Rich Farley, an author and partner at law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer who summed up the executive-suite dread. “In each case they’re too big to purge.”
Top executives simply “think extremism gets worse and will be inflamed by presidential candidates of both parties stalking out the populist ground both on the right and the left,” he added.
MAGA hasn’t been all bad for Wall Street and big business. President Trump can veto lefty stuff that gets to his desk over the next two years. It’s also hard to roll back his tax cuts and ramp up regulation with the White House in charge of regulatory agencies.
But MAGA is a broad coalition. Trump’s veep JD Vance may push for a more anti-business agenda in the wake of Democratic populists taking over in the House. Vance is expected to run for president in 2028, so now may be the time he cuts deals with Dems on certain issues to burnish a populist, anti-establishment rep, my sources say.
They don’t see Trump jettisoning his pro-tariff economic adviser Peter Navarro because Trump believes this stuff really works – even if all the evidence suggests it layered already high prices with a regressive tax and never produced the manufacturing boom he promised. Globalism isn’t making a comeback with this administration.
To be sure, Wall Street knows while Trumpism is a mixed bag, the Dem socialists offer something far worse. True, their obsession with higher taxes and regulation can be thwarted by Trump’s veto pen since the Senate doesn’t have a veto-proof Dem majority. That’s one bright spot.
But nothing the president can do will stop Senate and House investigations into everything, with his various business activities being at the top of the list. You might say the Democratic Socialists, the true lefties, make a small but vocal portion of the new party coalition, but the far left is its activist wing and it is ascendant.
So look for hearings into crypto (given the Trump family’s ties to this business) as well as Wall Street’s biggest money maker in years, AI, and whether the technology will eliminate jobs , carpet the nation with ugly, noisy, water-hogging data centers as it sets the stage for bots to rule the world.
Sign up to receive On The Money by Charlie Gasparino in your inbox every Thursday.
The latter might sound far fetched, but it’s exactly what the AI geeks like Anthropic’s Dario Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have weirdly been opining about even as they ask investors to finance their businesses ( Anthropic has just filed paperwork for an IPO ; as we have reported, OpenAI is weighing one in the first quarter of next year ).
Shares of AI-related companies, until recently, have been outperforming almost everything. A concerted effort by a Democratic-led Congress, stoked by Democratic Socialism, could put the finishing touches on the lancing of what many believe is a bubble in AI-related stocks, crashing an industry that has helped propel markets to record levels.
“It’s the era of overreach,” is how another C-suite type assesses what’s in store for big business no matter who’s in charge.

articles.title_orig: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux
articles.title_zh: OpenSSH Issues Emergency Fix for Flaw Letting Long Passwords Bypass SSH Auth on Alpine Linux
articles.content_orig:
Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.
OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16.
The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default.
The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project.
He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported.
Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true:
The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory.
On Alpine, accounts with no password set include:
Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas .
The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas . They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root.
Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no , and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $ -style password hash.
The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check.
OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server.
On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd:
Point releases 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 already include the fixed package. Branches 3.16 to 3.21 are past their end of support but also got fixed packages.
Cloud instances started from tiny-cloud images older than those point releases still need the update, or the setting below.
If you build OpenSSH yourself, version 10.6p2 includes the change, as its release notes describe.
If you cannot update yet, turning off password logins also stops the attack. First make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds. Then set PasswordAuthentication no , check the configuration with sshd -t , and restart sshd.
The advisory gives commands that add the setting in a drop-in file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d , which Alpine's default configuration reads from 3.19 onward. They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no , including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no .
The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine , root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys.
"If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says.
Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt() , the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field.
An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash.
For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored * , so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password.
This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks.
The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then.
The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem.
Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement , he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours.
No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.

articles.title_zh: John Deere Announces Iowa Plant Closures, Production Moves Through 2029
articles.content_orig:
